claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is dominated by a graded, Cu-enriched coating–substrate interfacial diffusion layer.
A Cu-enriched interfacial layer minimizes tensile–compression asymmetry.
The interfacial layer suppresses dislocation slip and twin formation at the interface.
Suppressing interfacial dislocation slip and twinning enhances high-temperature wear performance.
The baseline is an as-deposited, homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional metal substrate such as nickel.
Post-deposition annealing at approximately 600 °C promotes coating–substrate interdiffusion.
Post-deposition annealing at approximately 600 °C produces a graded, particularly Cu-enriched, interfacial layer.
The proposed comparison is between an as-deposited coating and a coating annealed at 600 °C.
The hypothesis is intended to apply near 600 °C under high normal loads.
A graded Cu-enriched interfacial layer reduces the mismatch in plastic deformation between the coating and substrate.
Local dislocation activity and twin formation are responsible for tensile–compression asymmetry at the coating–substrate interface.
Tensile–compression asymmetry in FeNiCrCoCu is sensitive to temperature and Cu content.
Mitigating tensile–compression asymmetry improves wear resistance under cyclic and sustained loading.
Annealed, interdiffused coatings should have significantly lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings.
Annealed, interdiffused coatings should have significantly lower friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings.
Annealed coatings should exhibit a distinct graded, Cu-enriched interfacial layer.
Annealed coatings should exhibit fewer indicators of interfacial dislocations and twins after high-temperature wear testing.
The as-deposited baseline lacks a pronounced interfacial diffusion layer.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to bulk material or low-temperature conditions where interfacial diffusion is less pronounced.
